data.raw_text:
Shimakaze during her trials, Miyazu Bay, Japan, 5 May 1943.

The IJN Shimakaze (島風, "Island Wind") was a one-of-a-kind experimental destroyer of the Imperial Japanese Navy during World War II, designed to be the fastest destroyer in the world at the time of her launch.

She was laid down in August 1941 at the Maizuru Naval Arsenal, launched in July 1942, and commissioned in May 1943. She was intended as the prototype for a new "Type C" destroyer class (Project Number F-52), but wartime resource shortages and shifting priorities meant no sister ships were ever built, leaving her as a unique vessel.

What made Shimakaze remarkable was her propulsion. She was equipped with experimental high-temperature, high-pressure steam turbines that produced about 79,240 shaft horsepower, far more than any other Japanese destroyer. On trials in 1943 she reached roughly 40.9 knots (about 75 km/h), making her one of the fastest destroyers ever built. Some sources note her trial speed was achieved at less than full displacement, but it remained an exceptional figure.

Her armament was also notable. She carried six 127 mm (5-inch) Type 3 dual-purpose guns in three twin turrets, a heavy anti-aircraft battery that grew over her career, and most distinctively, fifteen 610 mm (24-inch) torpedo tubes in three quintuple mounts, the heaviest torpedo armament ever fitted to a destroyer. These fired the famous Type 93 "Long Lance" oxygen-powered torpedoes, giving her tremendous offensive striking power against surface ships.

Her dimensions were roughly 129.5 m long with a standard displacement around 2,567 tons, and she had a complement of about 267 officers and men.

Operationally, Shimakaze served with the 2nd Destroyer Squadron and participated in several major late-war operations. She took part in the evacuation of Kiska in the Aleutians in July 1943, escorted carriers during the Battle of the Philippine Sea in June 1944, and fought in the Battle of Leyte Gulf in October 1944, including the action off Cape Engaño. She survived those engagements but was sunk on November 11, 1944, in Ormoc Bay off Leyte in the Philippines, when American carrier aircraft from Task Force 38 attacked a reinforcement convoy she was escorting (Operation TA). She was hit repeatedly, caught fire, and her torpedoes eventually detonated; she sank with heavy loss of life.

Shimakaze is often remembered as a "what-might-have-been" design, a glimpse of where Japanese destroyer development was heading before the war's industrial realities cut the program short. She has also become a popular subject in modern Japanese pop culture, particularly through the game Kantai Collection, where her character has made her one of the most recognizable IJN destroyer names outside historical circles.
